claim: Nuclear receptor corepressor 1 (NCOR1) controls naïve and effector Treg cell states.
source: Here, we reveal that nuclear receptor corepressor 1 (NCOR1) controls naïve and effector Treg cell states.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including flow cytometry and RNA-seq analyses.

claim: Upon NCOR1 deletion in T cells, effector Treg cell frequencies were elevated in mice.
source: Upon NCOR1 deletion in T cells, effector Treg cell frequencies were elevated in mice and in in vitro-generated human Treg cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1 demonstrating increased CD44hiCD62L- effector Treg cells in NCOR1-cKO mice.

claim: Upon NCOR1 deletion in T cells, effector Treg cell frequencies were elevated in in vitro-generated human Treg cells.
source: Upon NCOR1 deletion in T cells, effector Treg cell frequencies were elevated in mice and in in vitro-generated human Treg cells.
evidence: Supported by CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments in human CD4+ T cells shown in Figure 2.

claim: NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to protect mice from severe weight loss associated with CD4+ T cell transfer colitis.
source: NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to protect mice from severe weight loss and intestinal inflammation associated with CD4+ T cell transfer colitis, indicating impaired suppressive function.
evidence: Demonstrated by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 4 where mice receiving NCOR1-cKO Treg cells lost significantly more weight.

claim: NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to protect mice from intestinal inflammation associated with CD4+ T cell transfer colitis.
source: NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to protect mice from severe weight loss and intestinal inflammation associated with CD4+ T cell transfer colitis, indicating impaired suppressive function.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis showing disruption of crypt structures and enhanced T cell infiltration in Figure 4d.

claim: NCOR1-deficient Treg cells have impaired suppressive function.
source: NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to protect mice from severe weight loss and intestinal inflammation associated with CD4+ T cell transfer colitis, indicating impaired suppressive function.
evidence: Inferred from the failure to protect against colitis in the adoptive transfer model shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: NCOR1 controls the transcriptional integrity of Treg cells.
source: NCOR1 controls the transcriptional integrity of Treg cells, since effector gene signatures were already upregulated in naïve NCOR1-deficient Treg cells while effector NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to repress genes associated with naïve Treg cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6 demonstrating enrichment of effector signatures in naïve NCOR1-cKO Treg cells and naïve signatures in effector NCOR1-cKO Treg cells.

claim: Effector gene signatures were already upregulated in naïve NCOR1-deficient Treg cells.
source: NCOR1 controls the transcriptional integrity of Treg cells, since effector gene signatures were already upregulated in naïve NCOR1-deficient Treg cells while effector NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to repress genes associated with naïve Treg cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by GSEA showing enrichment of an 'effector Treg gene set' in naïve NCOR1-cKO Treg cells in Figure 6d.

claim: Effector NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to repress genes associated with naïve Treg cells.
source: NCOR1 controls the transcriptional integrity of Treg cells, since effector gene signatures were already upregulated in naïve NCOR1-deficient Treg cells while effector NCOR1-deficient Treg cells failed to repress genes associated with naïve Treg cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by GSEA showing enrichment of a 'naïve Treg gene set' in effector NCOR1-cKO Treg cells in Figure 6e.

claim: Genes related to cholesterol homeostasis including targets of liver X receptor (LXR) were dysregulated in NCOR1-deficient Treg cells.
source: Moreover, genes related to cholesterol homeostasis including targets of liver X receptor (LXR) were dysregulated in NCOR1-deficient Treg cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq pathway analysis showing upregulation of cholesterol biosynthesis pathways and LXR/RXR activation pathways in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genetic ablation of LXRβ in T cells did not revert the effects of NCOR1 deficiency on Treg cell subset composition.
source: However, genetic ablation of LXRβ in T cells did not revert the effects of NCOR1 deficiency, indicating that NCOR1 controls naïve and effector Treg cell subset composition independent from its ability to repress LXRβ-induced gene expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of NCOR1-LXRβ double knockout mice in Figure 7 showing persistent increase in effector Treg cells.

claim: NCOR1 controls naïve and effector Treg cell subset composition independent from its ability to repress LXRβ-induced gene expression.
source: However, genetic ablation of LXRβ in T cells did not revert the effects of NCOR1 deficiency, indicating that NCOR1 controls naïve and effector Treg cell subset composition independent from its ability to repress LXRβ-induced gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic experiments with NCOR1-LXRβ double knockout mice shown in Figure 7.

claim: NCOR1 maintains naïve and effector Treg cell states via regulating their transcriptional integrity.
source: Thus, our study reveals that NCOR1 maintains naïve and effector Treg cell states via regulating their transcriptional integrity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the RNA-seq data showing transcriptional dysregulation in NCOR1-deficient Treg cells.

claim: NCOR1 has a critical role in supporting the suppressive functions of Treg cells in vivo.
source: We also reveal a critical role for this epigenetic regulator in supporting the suppressive functions of Treg cells in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by the adoptive transfer colitis experiments in Figures 4 and 5 showing failure of NCOR1-deficient Treg cells to prevent disease.

claim: FOXP3+ regulatory T cells (Treg cells) are key for immune homeostasis.
source: FOXP3+ regulatory T cells (Treg cells) are key for immune homeostasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Deficiency or aberrant function of Treg cells triggers autoimmunity and inflammation.
source: Deficiency or aberrant function of Treg cells triggers autoimmunity and inflammation (Sakaguchi et al., 2020; Sumida et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The transcription factor FOXP3 is required for the generation, maintenance, and suppressive function of Treg cells.
source: The transcription factor FOXP3 is required for the generation, maintenance, and suppressive function of Treg cells, and loss of FOXP3 leads to fatal systemic autoimmunity in mice and humans (Hori et al., 2003; Fontenot et al., 2003; Khattri et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational studies on FOXP3.

claim: Loss of FOXP3 leads to fatal systemic autoimmunity in mice and humans.
source: The transcription factor FOXP3 is required for the generation, maintenance, and suppressive function of Treg cells, and loss of FOXP3 leads to fatal systemic autoimmunity in mice and humans (Hori et al., 2003; Fontenot et al., 2003; Khattri et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating the consequences of FOXP3 loss.

claim: Upon stimulation, naïve Treg cells undergo differentiation into effector Treg cells thereby acquiring distinct phenotypes and effector molecules expression.
source: Upon stimulation, naïve Treg cells (also known as resting Treg cells) undergo differentiation into effector Treg cells (also known as activated Treg cells) thereby acquiring distinct phenotypes and effector molecules expression (Cretney et al., 2013; Levine et al., 2014; Contreras-Castillo et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Treg cell differentiation.

claim: Effector Treg cells exhibit enhanced suppressive function compared to naïve Treg cells.
source: Effector Treg cells exhibit enhanced suppressive function compared to naïve Treg cells and maintain immune tolerance and homeostasis (Liston and Gray, 2014; Buszko and Shevach, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing effector Treg cell function.

claim: The conversion of naïve Treg cells into effector Treg cells is accompanied by metabolic reprogramming including relatively higher engagement of aerobic glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The conversion of naïve Treg cells into effector Treg cells is accompanied by metabolic reprogramming including relatively higher engagement of aerobic glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Treg cell metabolism cited in the introduction.

claim: The nuclear receptor co-repressor 1 (NCOR1) is a transcriptional regulator that bridges chromatin-modifying enzymes and transcription factors.
source: The nuclear receptor co-repressor 1 (NCOR1) is a transcriptional regulator that bridges chromatin-modifying enzymes and transcription factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NCOR1 function.

claim: NCOR1 mediates transcriptional repression of nuclear receptors such as thyroid hormone (TR), retinoic acid receptors (RAR), and liver X receptor (LXR) in the absence of their ligands.
source: NCOR1 mediates transcriptional repression of nuclear receptors (NRs) such as thyroid hormone (TR), retinoic acid receptors (RAR), and liver X receptor (LXR) in the absence of their ligands, via its interaction with members of the HDAC family, in particular, HDAC3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NCOR1 mechanism of action.

claim: NCOR1 mediates transcriptional repression via its interaction with members of the HDAC family, in particular, HDAC3.
source: NCOR1 mediates transcriptional repression of nuclear receptors (NRs) such as thyroid hormone (TR), retinoic acid receptors (RAR), and liver X receptor (LXR) in the absence of their ligands, via its interaction with members of the HDAC family, in particular, HDAC3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NCOR1 mechanism supported by citations.

claim: T cell-specific deletion of NCOR1 resulted in impaired survival of positively selected NCOR1-null TCRβhiCD69+/− thymocytes.
source: We and others have recently identified NCOR1 as an important regulator of T cell development, as T cell-specific deletion of NCOR1 resulted in impaired survival of positively selected NCOR1-null TCRβhiCD69+/− thymocytes.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors and others.

claim: NCOR1 deficiency leads to reduced numbers of peripheral T cells including Treg cells.
source: Furthermore, NCOR1 deficiency also leads to reduced numbers of peripheral T cells including Treg cells (Wang et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NCOR1 represses the pro-apoptotic factor BIM in double-positive thymocytes post-signaling, thereby affecting thymocyte survival during positive selection.
source: In addition, it was shown that NCOR1 represses the pro-apoptotic factor BIM in double-positive thymocytes post-signaling, thereby affecting thymocyte survival during positive selection (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: NCOR1 is essential for positive and negative selection during T cell development.
source: These data indicate that NCOR1 is essential for positive and negative selection during T cell development, as well as for the generation of the peripheral T cell pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies about NCOR1 function in thymocyte development.

claim: NCOR1 is essential for the generation of the peripheral T cell pool.
source: These data indicate that NCOR1 is essential for positive and negative selection during T cell development, as well as for the generation of the peripheral T cell pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies about NCOR1 function.

claim: NCOR1 regulates the transcriptional programs and effector functions of activated Th1 and Th17 cells.
source: Additionally, NCOR1 was shown to regulate the transcriptional programs and effector functions of activated Th1 and Th17 cells (Hainberger et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: There is an increase in the proportion of CD44hiCD62L– effector Treg cells in the spleen of NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: We observed an increase in the proportion of CD44hiCD62L– effector Treg cells and a corresponding decrease in CD44loCD62L+ naïve Treg cells in the spleen (Figure 1a and b)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1a and quantified in Figure 1b.

claim: There is a corresponding decrease in CD44loCD62L+ naïve Treg cells in the spleen of NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: We observed an increase in the proportion of CD44hiCD62L– effector Treg cells and a corresponding decrease in CD44loCD62L+ naïve Treg cells in the spleen (Figure 1a and b)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1a and quantified in Figure 1b.

claim: There is an increase in the proportion of CD44hiCD62L– effector Treg cells in lymph nodes of NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: We observed an increase in the proportion of CD44hiCD62L– effector Treg cells and a corresponding decrease in CD44loCD62L+ naïve Treg cells in the spleen (Figure 1a and b), Lymph node (LN) and mesenteric LN (mLN) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b) in the absence of NCOR1.

claim: There is an increase in the proportion of CD44hiCD62L– effector Treg cells in mesenteric lymph nodes of NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: We observed an increase in the proportion of CD44hiCD62L– effector Treg cells and a corresponding decrease in CD44loCD62L+ naïve Treg cells in the spleen (Figure 1a and b), Lymph node (LN) and mesenteric LN (mLN) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b) in the absence of NCOR1.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: The relative increase in effector Treg cells in NCOR1-cKO mice correlated with an elevated expression of KLRG1 in Treg cells.
source: The relative increase in effector Treg cells in NCOR1-cKO mice also correlated with an elevated expression of KLRG1 and CD69 in Treg cells, two markers characteristic of activated/effector Treg cells (Yu et al., 2018; Dias et al., 2017; Cortés et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2012)

claim: The relative increase in effector Treg cells in NCOR1-cKO mice correlated with an elevated expression of CD69 in Treg cells.
source: The relative increase in effector Treg cells in NCOR1-cKO mice also correlated with an elevated expression of KLRG1 and CD69 in Treg cells, two markers characteristic of activated/effector Treg cells (Yu et al., 2018; Dias et al., 2017; Cortés et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2012)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: KLRG1 and CD69 are markers characteristic of activated/effector Treg cells.
source: The relative increase in effector Treg cells in NCOR1-cKO mice also correlated with an elevated expression of KLRG1 and CD69 in Treg cells, two markers characteristic of activated/effector Treg cells (Yu et al., 2018; Dias et al., 2017; Cortés et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing these markers.

claim: The proportion of CD25+ cells within the FOXP3+ Treg cell population was decreased in NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: while the proportion of CD25+ cells within the FOXP3+ Treg cell population was decreased.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: There were higher percentages of ICOS-expressing Treg cells in NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: Moreover, we detected higher percentages of ICOS-expressing Treg cells in NCOR1-cKO mice, and NCOR1-deficient Treg cells expressed elevated levels of GITR in LN and mLN.

claim: NCOR1-deficient Treg cells expressed elevated levels of GITR in LN and mLN.

claim: There was no significant difference in the expression of CTLA4 between WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells.
source: There was no significant difference in the expression of CTLA4 between WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: The total numbers of naïve and effector Treg cells were reduced in NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: However, the total numbers of naïve and effector Treg cells were reduced in NCOR1-cKO mice (Figure 1c).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification in Figure 1c.

claim: The reduction in total Treg cell numbers in NCOR1-cKO mice is caused by the drop in total CD4+ T cells as well as the relative reduction of Treg cells within the CD4+ T cell population.
source: This is due to the overall reduction in Treg cell numbers, caused by the drop in total CD4+ T cells as well as the relative reduction of Treg cells within the CD4+ T cell population in NCOR1-cKO mice, as previously reported (Müller et al., 2017; Hainberger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data and previous reports cited.

claim: The percentage of Treg cells expressing Ki67 was similar between splenic WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells.
source: The percentage of Treg cells expressing Ki67, a marker associated with cell proliferation, as well as the expression levels of Ki67 (gMFI) in FOXP3+ cells, was similar between splenic WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b.

claim: The expression levels of Ki67 (gMFI) in FOXP3+ cells was similar between splenic WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells.
source: The percentage of Treg cells expressing Ki67, a marker associated with cell proliferation, as well as the expression levels of Ki67 (gMFI) in FOXP3+ cells, was similar between splenic WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b.

claim: There was no difference in the viability of WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells at steady state.
source: Similarly, there was no difference in the viability of WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells (see timepoint 0 hr; Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Treg cell proliferation at a steady state is not controlled by NCOR1.
source: These data suggest that Treg cell proliferation and survival at a steady state are not controlled by NCOR1.

claim: Treg cell survival at a steady state is not controlled by NCOR1.
source: These data suggest that Treg cell proliferation and survival at a steady state are not controlled by NCOR1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Ki67 and viability data.

claim: There was no increase in CD44hiCD62L– effector cell subsets within the FOXP3– CD4+ T cell population in NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: Of note, there was no increase in CD44hiCD62L– effector cell subsets within the FOXP3– CD4+ T cell population, in fact, effector subsets were slightly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d.

claim: Effector subsets within the FOXP3– CD4+ T cell population were slightly reduced in NCOR1-cKO mice.
source: Of note, there was no increase in CD44hiCD62L– effector cell subsets within the FOXP3– CD4+ T cell population, in fact, effector subsets were slightly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d.

source: Taken together, the flow cytometry analysis indicates that the deletion of NCOR1 in T cells changes the ratio of naïve to effector Treg cells at a steady state.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1.

claim: T follicular regulatory (Tfr) cells represent a subset of peripheral effector Treg cells that are induced during an immune response.
source: T follicular regulatory (Tfr) cells represent a subset of peripheral effector Treg cells that are induced during an immune response.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tfr cells.

source: Tfr cells are defined as CXCR5+PD1+CD44hi CD4+ T cells that express FOXP3 (Wollenberg et al., 2011; Linterman et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies defining Tfr cells.

claim: Similar percentages of CXCR5+PD1+CD44hi T follicular helper (Tfh) cells were induced within the CD4+ T cell population in WT and NCOR1-cKO mice after immunization.
source: After immunization, similar percentages of CXCR5+PD1+CD44hi T follicular helper (Tfh) cells were induced within the CD4+ T cell population in WT and NCOR1-cKO mice (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1e and f.

claim: The frequency of Tfr cells was higher in NCOR1-cKO mice after immunization.
source: In contrast, the frequency of Tfr cells was higher in NCOR1-cKO mice (Figure 1e and f)

claim: The total number of CXCR5+PD1+CD44hi Tfh cells was slightly reduced in the absence of NCOR1 after immunization.
source: The total number of CXCR5+PD1+CD44hi Tfh cells was slightly reduced in the absence of NCOR1, while Tfr cell numbers were similar between WT and NCOR1-cKO mice (Figure 1g).

claim: Tfr cell numbers were similar between WT and NCOR1-cKO mice after immunization.
source: The total number of CXCR5+PD1+CD44hi Tfh cells was slightly reduced in the absence of NCOR1, while Tfr cell numbers were similar between WT and NCOR1-cKO mice (Figure 1g).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification in Figure 1g.

claim: CD25 expression was decreased in CXCR5+PD1+CD44hiFOXP3+ Tfr cells isolated from NCOR1-cKO mice compared to WT mice after immunization.

claim: The most mature Tfr cells in the germinal center downregulate CD25.
source: in line with the observation that the most mature Tfr cells in the germinal center downregulate CD25 (Wing et al., 2017).

source: Together, this data suggests that NCOR1 restrains the generation of activated/effector Treg cells not only at a steady state but also upon immunization.

source: Despite a trend for higher levels of phospho-ERKT202/Y204, phospho-AKTS473 and phospho-S6S240/244 in NCOR1-cKO Treg cells at several early time points, we only observed a significant difference for phospho-AKTS473 at the 2 hr timepoint, which might indicate altered mTORC2 activation (Sarbassov et al., 2005; Szwed et al., 2021).

claim: The significant difference in phospho-AKTS473 at the 2 hr timepoint might indicate altered mTORC2 activation in NCOR1-cKO Treg cells.
source: Despite a trend for higher levels of phospho-ERKT202/Y204, phospho-AKTS473 and phospho-S6S240/244 in NCOR1-cKO Treg cells at several early time points, we only observed a significant difference for phospho-AKTS473 at the 2 hr timepoint, which might indicate altered mTORC2 activation (Sarbassov et al., 2005; Szwed et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation based on the phospho-AKT data and knowledge of mTORC2 signaling.

claim: There was no significant difference in the viability of WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells after 4 or 24 hr of activation.

claim: There was a decrease in the percentage of viable NCOR1-cKO Treg cells after 72 hr of activation.
source: While there was no significant difference in the viability of WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells after 4 or 24 hr of activation, we observed a decrease in the percentage of viable NCOR1-cKO Treg cells after 72 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claim: NCOR1-cKO Treg cells might display a slightly higher transient degree of activation after TCR triggering but their viability declines a few days later.
source: Overall, these data suggest that NCOR1-cKO Treg cells might display a slightly higher transient degree of activation after TCR triggering but their viability declines a few days later.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phospho-flow and viability data.

claim: There was no difference in FOXP3 expression between WT and NCOR1-deficient iTreg cells.

claim: Upregulation of CD44 and ICOS in NCOR1-cKO iTreg cells suggests enhanced effector features in the absence of NCOR1.

claim: iTreg cells downregulate FOXP3 upon restimulation with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 in the absence of TGFβ.
source: iTreg cells are known to downregulate FOXP3 upon restimulation with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 in the absence of TGFβ (Floess et al., 2007).

source: There was no difference in the downregulation of FOXP3 between WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells, indicating that NCOR1 function is dispensable for the maintenance of FOXP3 expression in iTreg cells (Figure 2c).

claim: NCOR1 function is dispensable for the maintenance of FOXP3 expression in iTreg cells.
source: There was no difference in the downregulation of FOXP3 between WT and NCOR1-cKO Treg cells, indicating that NCOR1 function is dispensable for the maintenance of FOXP3 expression in iTreg cells (Figure 2c).

claim: CD27 is a marker associated with a naïve phenotype in CD4+ T cells.

evidence: This is speculation based on the MYC target gene enrichment and the phenotype of NCOR1-deficient Treg cells.

source: Of note, while LXRβ-cKO mice also displayed higher MYC protein levels in effector Treg cells relative to their WT counterparts, this was reverted in NCOR1-LXRβ-cDKO animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 3a).

claim: Deletion of NCOR1 led to an increase in the fraction of human CD4+ T cells expressing high levels of MYC under Treg-inducing conditions.

evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3b and c.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the genetic experiments with LXRβ and NCOR1/LXRβ knockout mice.
